items.text: **The identity contract said both that an unverified guest buys and that it cannot.** `verifyGuestEmail`: *"Unverified accounts still buy. Blocking purchase on verification loses the sale"*; `registerGuest` and `GuestSession.isVerified`: *"an unverified account may browse but not transact"*. **The requirement matrix adds a third constraint**: 2.6.28 *"An online sale can be done using Guest Checkout or Registration on the website or Login to SSO. This should be configurable per site"*, and 2.6.67 lists Guest Checkout among the B2C logins; the minutes' reference checkout is *"cart summary → login/guest checkout with dual OTP validation"*. A decision unblocks the cart and checkout screens and `checkoutCart`'s refusals. **Decided 17 September: no order against an unproven contact.** On the guest web and app the site's existing `guestCheckout` feature decides, **off by default**: off, the guest signs in verified before the cart; on, a guest without an account proves the email or mobile with a one-time code at checkout. **The kiosk is exempt** — a walk-up takes printed tickets, so there is no address to prove. Written into `identity`, `orders` (`checkoutCart` 403) and `white-label`, and onto `WEB-010`/`GST-041` and their sign-in screens. **Refined 18 September by [ADR-0045](../adr/0045-every-order-carries-a-proven-contact.md), which corrected the placement and added what the 17 September rule left out.** **The gate is the checkout page, not the cart** — matrix 2.6.1 §2.4 reads *"On the check out page, users can log in or manually fill in the following details: name, email, mobile number, nationality"*, and §2.3 offers *"Add to Cart or proceed directly to check out"*. The 17 September edit had walled the cart, which also breaks 2.6.45's abandoned-cart reminder by leaving only identified guests able to abandon one. `WEB-010 → WEB-016` is removed and the fork moves to `WEB-011 Guest Details & Attendee Forms`, which *is* the page 2.6.1 describes; `GST-041 Checkout Entry` was already it. **And the profile half was never decided**: both routes produce a durable guest profile, a one-time checkout profile carries no credential (2.6.29 — access needs a login to recall previous transactions), and a returning verified contact **attaches the order to the profile already held and does not open it** (2.6.1's 22.2.8 automatic resolution, bounded). Matrix **22.2.8 and 7.3.7 contradict each other** — automatic merge versus authorised-user merge with audit and rollback — and both hold: automatic where the evidence is a code the guest just entered, staff-reviewed where it is an inference from passport, national id, an unproved phone or a similar name. Closed.

items.text: **A third of the API surface is a provisional draft named after a screen title, and the count is exact.** Measured 8 September: **577 of the package's 1,626 operations carry `x-ticvai-provisional: true`, and for all 577 — every single one — the `summary` is verbatim the title of the screen in its own `x-ticvai-consumed-by`.** Not most of them; all of them. The operations state it themselves: *"Drafted from the workshop pack; the shape below is read out of it, not invented... Still provisional. A shape read out of a PDF has not been agreed with anyone who has to build it, and the schema says so in its own persistence tag: it is a request, not a table."* **This is the same defect as the 423 title-stamped screens, one layer down**, and the two corroborate each other in the way that proves nothing: `check-screens` verifies that every screen's operations resolve to a contract, and 577 of those contracts were written from the screens. **Two derived artefacts agreeing is not corroboration** — Claude Design's own caution about the layout check, arriving from the contract side. **It is why CF-170's Class B cannot be fixed by adding operations** and why any count of *contracted* coverage is 35% softer than it reads. **Audited against the source packs 8 September, and the 577 are sound.** Every provisional description cites its origin as `<pack>, page N`. Checked against the 39 client Design Books in `OneDrive_1_8-9-2026.zip`: **577 of 577 citations resolve to a real pack, and not one cites a page beyond that pack's length** — 573 distinct pages across 17 books, maximum cited page inside the book's page count in every case. **They are not invented and they are not unverifiable.** The `provisional` flag means *not yet agreed with whoever builds it*, which is an honest label rather than a defect, and the summaries matching screen titles is what you get when a screen and an operation are read out of the same page of the same pack. **The real gap is the other direction, and it is larger: 22 of the 39 Design Books have no operation drafted from them at all** — 1,323 pages of client design material against 1,058 pages that were used. The biggest untouched are Retail (202pp), Inventory & Procurement (175pp), Resource Management (169pp), F&B Backend (130pp), Wallet (129pp) and Finance (123pp) — **which is CF-164 and CF-125 seen from the source side**: the F&B/Retail/Procurement/Inventory workshop that is outstanding in three consecutive MoMs is exactly the material nobody has drafted from. **Recommendation: stop treating the 577 as the problem.** Schedule the workshops to agree them, and open the 22 uncited books as the scoping question they actually are

items.text: **Seventeen screens promise a publication their declared operations cannot perform, and five of them are a broken workflow rather than a naming defect.** Found by Claude Design 8 September, extending the rule package-wide from the nine already recorded. **Class B is the one to raise first: five screens can approve and cannot publish** — `BO-293` Membership Product Validation, `BO-353` Multi-Media Preview, `ADM-247` Versioning & Governance, `CMS-030` Privacy Configuration Testing and `CMS-050` Waiver Approval each declare only an `approve*` operation against a title ending in *Publication*. **An approval with nothing to release is a dead end in the workflow**, not a name to tidy: somebody signs off and the thing they signed off cannot go live. **Class A is eleven title-only screens** declaring a single `list*` — `BO-173`, `BO-193`, `BO-203`, `BO-213`, `BO-223`, `BO-233`, `ADM-085`, `ADM-143`, `ADM-227`, `ADM-307`, `CMS-033` — which is re-signature work and is why the six of them in the 8 September patch were correctly held rather than given `publishGate`. **Class C is one screen that monitors what it creates**: `ADM-115 Live Dynamic Price Execution & Deployment Monitor` declares `createLiveDynamicPrice`. **Class D is one false positive to exclude**: `ADM-029 Deployment Monitor` declares `startRollout`, `pauseRollout` and `rollbackRollout` and is a real deployment actor — the rule caught it because rollout control is not named `publish*`. **Each class needs a different remedy**, which is the reason for classing them: B needs operations added to contracts, A needs titles or operations decided, C needs one of the two names changed, D needs nothing. **Recommendation: take Class B first** — it is five contract additions against a workflow that currently cannot complete **Checked 8 September, and Class B is not five contract additions. Do not add the operations.** All five `approve*` operations carry `x-ticvai-provisional: true` and `tags: [drafted]`, and **every one of their summaries is verbatim the title of the screen that consumes it** — `approveMembershipProductValidation` summarises as *Membership Product Validation, Approval, Publication & Versioning*. Their own descriptions say so: *"drafted from the workshop pack... a shape read out of a PDF has not been agreed with anyone who has to build it."* **So the approval step does not exist either** — the operation naming it is a provisional draft named after the screen, which is Class A's defect one layer down in the contracts. Adding five `publish*` siblings would invent agreed API surface on top of unagreed drafts. **The remedy is to de-provisionalise the five with someone who has to build them**, and the publication either falls out of that conversation or the titles were wrong. See CF-171 for the population this belongs to

items.text: **Three places where the data model was built and no screen was ever written, and one where the reverse is true.** ADR-0041 turns 57 command centres into rows in `reporting.dashboard`, which needs **three or four authoring screens that do not exist**: a dashboard list separating mine from shared, an editor that adds a tile and binds it to a `report_definition`, a tile configuration panel for `visualisation`, `parameters` and `refresh_seconds`, and a viewer if the editor is not also one. Searching all 1,091 screen names for `widget`, `saved view`, `drag`, `layout editor` or `add a tile` returns **nothing**, while the tables, the four operations and a `tiles` array capped at 24 all exist. **Two further decisions ride on it**: the editor must surface `dashboard.aggregate_cost` and `report_definition.estimated_cost`, because 24 tiles on a short refresh is a performance incident nobody was warned about; and there is no `deleteDashboard` — `list`, `create`, `get`, `update` and nothing else — so a soft or hard delete has to be chosen where `is_shared` is true. **The same shape appears twice more, from the other side**: `seatp` has 13 boards and 130 screens of seat-map authoring with no package counterpart at all — no `canvas`, `section`, `suite` or `seating chart` screen exists against a `seating` schema of 14 tables — and `crm` has a Guest Directory, Activity Timeline and Corporate & Groups the package never specified. **Design that exists and specs that do not, next to specs that exist and screens that do not.** Recommendation: take the four dashboard screens as the first tranche, since the contract and DDL are already there and it unblocks deleting 57

items.text: **A region may now hold more than one Postgres instance, and nothing decides which one a new tenant lands on.** ADR-0040 removed the ceiling by letting a cell add an instance, and left two things open that only a person can settle. **First, the trigger**: sustained concurrent server connections is the signal, but not the number — too low and a region grows hosts it does not need, too high and the first symptom is a Saturday evening. **Second, placement**: fullest-first packs tenants and leaves the last instance underused; emptiest-first spreads them and makes every instance equally busy; pinned lets a client buy a quiet neighbour and is the one a sales conversation will ask for. They diverge on the day a tenant grows, which is the day the choice is expensive to change. **Blocked behind this: `control.cell_instance` and an `instance_id` on `control.cell_tenant`** — without them a database name is not an address and the router cannot find a tenant on the second instance. **Recommendation: emptiest-first with a pin override.** It is the only one that degrades gently, and the pin is what a dedicated client is actually buying **Decided 8 September by [ADR-0042](../adr/0042-when-a-region-grows-and-where-a-tenant-lands.md), and it stays open on one number.** The recommendation is taken: placement is emptiest-first with a pin, where *emptiest* is **peak concurrent server connections over the trailing 7 days as a fraction of that instance's own `max_connections`** — not a count of databases, which would place a tenant onto the host with ten quiet neighbours and away from the one with three busy ones. The schema gap is closed with it: `control.cell_instance` exists and `cell_tenant.instance_id` is **required from the first row**, while every region still has one instance, because a column populated only once there are two is a column every reader guesses about — and the guess is wrong exactly once, on the first region that grows. **The trigger's shape is decided and its threshold is not**: add an instance when peak connections hold at or above **70%** of `max_connections` on three days in a rolling seven, at least two non-consecutive — three-in-seven separates a level that has moved from a concert, and a single five-minute period above 90% pages rather than provisions. **The 70% is the sign-off**: 89% is one busy tenant from exhaustion and adding an instance is a host, a template, a fan-out and a move, so the gap between the two is the runway, and how much runway to buy is a judgement rather than arithmetic

items.text: **The control plane holds personal data before a tenant exists, and it is also the thing that sits above every region.** Two sources want it in two places. `control.onboarding_application` carries `company_name`, `contact_email`, `contact_phone` and `country_code` — **a prospect's contact details, recorded before there is a tenant to own them** — which under a residency commitment belongs in the prospect's jurisdiction. ADR-0010 §1 puts the Guest Link Registry *"in the Control Plane, pseudonymous only"* and orchestrates cross-region redemption *"from the Control Plane by `guestLinkId`, fanning out to each linked cell"* — **which needs one control plane above all regions, not one inside each.** ADR-0038 made residency structural by giving each region its own Postgres instance, and ADR-0039 gives the control plane a database of its own without saying how many of them there are. **A decision unblocks the provisioning script**, which has to connect to a control database by name, and the `control.cell` relation, which either lists every region's cells or only its own. **Recommendation: split on personal data, which is the line ADR-0023 and ADR-0010 already draw.** One global control plane holding what must be global and carries no personal data — the cell registry, placement, releases, licences, the pseudonymous Guest Link Registry — and a regional control database for anything with a natural person in it, onboarding applications first. The cost is one more database per region and a `control` schema that is read from two places; the alternative is either a prospect's phone number in the wrong country or a cross-region registry that cannot see across regions **Decided 8 September by [ADR-0043](../adr/0043-the-control-plane-splits-on-personal-data.md). Closed.** The recommendation is taken and **it is far cheaper than this entry assumed**: counting the columns rather than arguing from the shape, **only three of the 50 `control` tables carry a natural person inline** — `onboarding_application` (`contact_email`, `contact_phone`), `developer_account` (`contact_email`) and `tenant` (`billing_email`). The schema was already careful: `control.partner_user` holds a `principal_id` and not a name, which is the pattern the decision generalises. So `control` stays global with 47 tables including the cell registry and the pseudonymous Guest Link Registry, and a `control_regional` per region takes `onboarding_application` whole plus two extracted columns. **The rule, not the list, is the decision**: a table goes regional when its *subject* is a natural person, and otherwise stays global with the personal column extracted — moving every table that merely contains personal data would take `tenant` with it, and a tenant record in one region is a platform that cannot see its own customers. **The cost is one instance outside every region**, because a global control plane hosted inside a region turns that region's outage into a platform outage

To illustrate the scale difference, Qossai gave two contrasting examples: a stadium such as Real Madrid's (~60,000 seats) could sell out within a few hours of tickets going live for a major event, generating extremely high concurrent load, whereas a client like a water park or museum might see a maximum of around 2,000 visitors per day — a much lower and steadier load (roughly five people per minute). items.text: **The delivery plan prices 7,552 person-days and its priorities contradict the dependency order the walk found.** `sources/planning/TAIS_Product_Planning_and_Delivery_Plan_4_1.xlsx` had never entered the package either — 23 epics, 445 features, 2,173 tasks, a milestone plan, a dependency matrix and a Jira import, covering 3,332 requirements. **It is a good document and two things in it need reconciling.** **(1) Resource Management is P3 — Could, at 63 matrix requirements**, and it is the single most-depended-on gap in the walk: CF-125 is cited by rows in five domains, and rentals, lockers, cabanas, instructor assignment, event resourcing, maintenance resource planning and 7.6's fifteen-row rental module all sit behind it. **A P3 prerequisite blocks every P1 that needs it.** **Access Control System is also P3 at 114 requirements**, which reads as a scoring artefact rather than a judgement — `access` is one of the best-covered contracts in the package and gate entry is the operational core. **(2) The plan splits one module across three priorities** — Notifications and Messaging appears at P1, P2 and P3; Loyalty at P1, P2 and P3; Portfolio at P1, P2 and P3; Digital Waivers at P1 and P2 — so a module is partly must-have and partly could-have, which is not a schedulable statement. **The plan's own *Missing Components* sheet independently reaches several of the walk's conclusions** — ABAC policy engine (CF-130), central monitoring and alerting (CF-134), a single notification service (BL-052), developer portal and OpenAPI docs (CF-135), performance budget (BL-098) — and marks **DevOps/IaC and CI/CD as outright MISSING**, which matches the package holding no SQL, no code and no Sprint 0. **Recommendation: re-derive priority from the dependency matrix rather than from requirement counts**, and reconcile against the 178 backlog entries before the plan is used to schedule anything **Deferred to the reconciliation — Chinmay, 18 August.** Finished once the milestone-to-wave reconciliation is done. **Resource Management's P3 rating is already resolved**: CF-125 puts it in scope, which was half of this conflict.

items.text: **The platform cannot issue a tax invoice, and in the UAE that is a VAT obligation rather than a document feature.** 5.7.93 requires tax invoices, simplified invoices, corporate invoices and consolidated invoices; 5.7.94 requires full and partial credit memos linked to them; 5.10.3 requires the receipt to show *"all required fields in accordance with VAT regulations"* and **nothing anywhere states what those fields are.** `finance` is otherwise strong here — `LegalEntity` carries `taxRegistrationNumber`, `countryCode`, `currencyScale` and `fiscalYearStartMonth`; `TaxCode` supports compound tax, inclusive and exclusive treatment and effective dating; the ledger is append-only with reversal rather than edit. **The data exists and the document does not.** `subscription.generateInvoice` bills a tenant for the platform, which is a different payer, a different ledger and a different format. **Three things make this a decision rather than a build item.** A UAE tax invoice has a **mandated format** — supplier TRN, sequential numbering that cannot gap, prescribed fields, Arabic where required — and issuing a non-compliant one is a finding at audit, not a formatting complaint. **A credit memo is the paired obligation**: a refund against a tax invoice is not simply a reversing journal, it is a document with its own sequence. And **sequential numbering interacts with ADR-0013 and ADR-0014** — a local-first till that journals offline and a cell-per-region topology both make a single gapless sequence harder than it looks, and the answer differs by whether numbering is per legal entity, per venue or per till. **Also unresolved: e-invoicing.** The UAE is phasing in mandatory e-invoicing, and whether that binds in the delivery window is a question for the client's finance function rather than for us **To Qossai and finance — Chinmay, 18 August.** The open question is what a UAE tax invoice must contain: **5.10.3 requires *all required fields in accordance with VAT regulations* and nothing states what those fields are.** `finance` already carries the TRN, compound tax and inclusive treatment; the gap is the document.

items.text: **Cookie consent management is fifteen requirements, a regulatory obligation, and normally bought rather than built.** 2.6.51–2.6.65 ask for a consent banner with configurable layouts and languages, cookie categorisation into strictly-necessary, functional, analytics and marketing, **automatic site scanning to detect new and third-party cookies, pixel tags and tracking technologies**, script blocking so analytics and advertising tags do not load before consent, a preference centre, consent records with timestamp and identifier, an audit trail of withdrawals, multi-domain preference sharing, consent analytics and an administration portal. **2.6.60 names GDPR, the ePrivacy Directive, CCPA, CPRA, LGPD and PDPL**, so this is compliance rather than preference. **The package has one trace: `PolicyKind.cookie`, a policy document a tenant can publish.** That is the text, not the enforcement. **`marketing-crm` does hold a real PDPL consent register** — purposes of marketing, personalisation, profiling, thirdPartySharing, aiProcessing and transactional, with `noticeVersion`, `expiresAfterMonths`, `isRequiredForService`, source per channel and full history — **and it answers a different question.** Consent to process a guest's data for marketing is not consent to set a tracking cookie on a browser, the legal bases differ, and the second has to be enforced client-side before a script loads. **The decision is build, buy or drop.** Cookie scanning means maintaining a cookie database and re-scanning as third-party tags change, which is the product OneTrust and Cookiebot sell; building it is a standing maintenance commitment on a platform whose scope is venue operations. Buying it means a vendor on every tenant storefront and a data-residency question under ADR-0009. **Dropping it is only available if no tenant storefront sets a non-essential cookie**, which the analytics requirements elsewhere in the matrix contradict **To Qossai — Chinmay, 18 August.** Cookie consent is a buy-or-build decision, not a design one, and **script blocking is the part that makes it a product rather than a form.** OneTrust and Cookiebot exist.

Key concern: virtual queue guests must not be merged into the same physical line as VIP guests, since VIP guests pay specifically to minimize their wait and enter within minutes of arriving — mixing the two would erode the VIP guest's paid value. A virtual queue guest, while not waiting in a physical line, has still effectively “waited” (e.g., 60 minutes) before their return window, so the operational model needs its own dedicated handling at the ride (e.g., a separate line, or scanning a QR code within a specific arrival window) distinct from both VIP and walk-in guests.

Resource management is an optional module for tracking bookable resources tied to a product or package — for example, a desert excursion package that requires both a vehicle and a driver. A resource "template" defines the required resource types for a given product; individual resources (specific vehicles, named drivers) are listed and can be scheduled with an availability calendar/roster (marking specific dates as unavailable). items.text: Answered by the 14 August MoM section 10, which this question was waiting for. Parking is barrier integration, in three models, and it is not space counting. (1) No integration - TICVAI issues its own QR and on-site security verifies it manually; (2) ANPR - the guest enters a plate at checkout and TICVAI pushes it to the parking system's whitelist so the barrier opens; (3) QR handoff - TICVAI sends a QR to the barrier for validation. Pay-per-hour parking is explicitly out of scope, handled by the parking vendor's own POS. So this is one configuration screen choosing a model and binding a vendor adaptor, not the three different screens the question feared - and ADR-0012's adaptor-first rule is what the minute asks for when it says a new parking vendor should take days rather than weeks. The `parking` module key in the White Label Builder now has something behind it.

hits.paragraph: Chinmay and Qossai reviewed three parking integration models: (1) no integration — TICVAI issues its own QR code and on-site security manually verifies it; (2) ANPR/plate-number integration — the guest enters their plate number at checkout, and TICVAI's API pushes the plate number to the parking system's whitelist so the barrier opens automatically; (3) QR-code handoff — TICVAI sends a QR code to the parking system's barrier for entry validation. A separate, pay-per-hour parking model (unrelated to ticketing) can be handled independently via the parking system's own POS. Qossai noted the team has integrated with such parking APIs before (consuming and pushing data) and that the architecture

Parking: Two supported models: (1) fully platform-native — guest purchases parking, receives a QR code scanned by a handheld device at the gate; (2) integrated with a third-party parking/ANPR system — guest enters their plate number, which is whitelisted so the barrier opens automatically on arrival. Both flows are to be supported in the app.

Chinmay opened by referencing the requirement matrix's "one user per session" rule for the POS and asked how breaks — where a live cashier needs to step away — should be handled. Allam confirmed the model: the logged-in user must either log out or suspend their shift before a second user can log into the same workstation; the workstation and user session are tied together, so no second user can log in over an active session. Qossai confirmed this matches the intended meaning of "one user, one session" — a user can take a break and a different user can log in afterward, but never concurrently on the same workstation.
